Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Due to fire suppression and a lack of active forest management in the Fort Meade
Recreation Area (FMRA), the forest, rangeland, and ecosystem structure and health has
been declining. Currently, the forested areas of the Fort Meade Recreation Area are
susceptible to catastrophic wildfires. If this happens, a catastrophic wildfire would
threaten lives, consume property, and have a negative impact on the ecosystem and
historic value of the area. Management of these ecosystems will promote a healthy,
diverse, and resilient landscape that could be maintained and used for recreation for
generations to come.
With multiple resource management goals and objectives, the proposed treatments would
maintain and improve the ecological structure and aesthetic values of both the forested
and rangeland areas of the Fort Meade Recreation Area, while enhancing watershed
values and wildlife habitat. A primary goal of ecological restoration is to reverse the
decline of ecosystem health by restoring the structure and function. Ecological
restoration is also referred to as the process of renewing and maintaining ecosystem
health. The focus of ecosystem management is on long term ecosystem sustainability.
By protecting forests and grasslands from unnaturally intensive and destructive wildfires,
the conditions of our public lands are improved, firefighter and public safety improves,
and the landscape attributes valued by society are conserved.

Objectives:
Conduct all burn activities in a safe and efficient manner.
Confine the fire to the burn unit.
Under burn a minimum 75% of Ponderosa Pine stands.

 Top kill a minimum of 50% of the juniper and Douglas fir less than 3" dbh.

Planned_Implementation:
A test fire will be conducted by ground crews, on the up hill I down wind side of the unit as directed by the RXB2
and if results are satisfactory firing will commence into the wind I down slope in order to initiate a backing fire and
to begin establishing black lines. Black lining may be conducted by the holding forces and will consist of an ignition
team progressing along each flank. As black lines attain sufficient depth, or it becomes apparent that the majority of
the burn unit perimeter will not support fire spread due to sparse, and or, green fuels then Aerial ignition of the
interior may begin at the direction of the Burn Boss/FIRB. The Aerial ignition operation will concentrate on the
North facing timbered slopes and will consist of running strips on the contour across the slope, beginning at the top
and progressing down slope I up wind whenever possible. The preferred sequence for Aerial ignition of the interior
would be to lag behind black lining operations, and progress down slope toward Lion coulee. Communication
between Ground and Aerial resources will be maintained at all times for safety and to coordinate between ignition
and holding forces. Firing will continue along the flanks of the unit as directed by the RXBB/FIRB. Aerial Ignition
will be done using PSD.
Actual_Implementation:
Lion Coulee EAST Unit 1 – Days 1 and 2: (Narrative provided by Jennifer Walker)
• Needle litter carried fire nicely except during early mornings. Adequate consumption of 1hr and 10hr fuels.
• Herbaceous green-up was advanced (cool season grasses were in flowering stage), but old litter carried fire through green during daytime
operations. Even so, ignitions had to focus on more receptive fuels in timbered areas.
• All conifers were actively growing from recent bud-break so were reluctant to sustain fire; but plentiful juniper ladder fuels with needle litter
contributed to isolated torching of canopy trees. There were very long lag periods for heat buildup prior to torch-outs, so igniters had difficulty
judging the timing of their dots/strips. The isolated torching contributed to scorching of adjacent trees and associated mortality of those trees.
Lion Coulee EAST Unit 1 – Day 3: (Narrative provided by Karly Krausz)
Fire behavior and effects were variable, dependent of fuel bed:
• Overall, fire behavior was more favorable this day, than the two previous days. There was generally less isolated torching in the timber.
Fire carried through the grass and needle litter by mid-morning. There was also adequate consumption of 1- and 10-hour fuels.
• Two firing operations took place during this burn period. One small operation on the north flank and the other, larger operation on the
south flank. Although observations were taken at both sites during the day, most of the observations were taken on the south flank.
• At 1057 hours, the south flank had increased isolated torching and fire carried more through the grasses than just a few hours prior. I
observed pockets of regeneration torching/consumed. Juniper was readily consumed. On the north flank, ignition operations were just
getting started.
• At 1155, the north flank operations were in full swing, the blackline on north flank is wide and appears to be complete from K-F. Crews
continue to reinforce K-F down the slope. The south flank continues to have some isolated torching. Crews used firing pistol to ignite
deep draws, while others hand-lite to reinforce pistol operations. Smoke dispersal is to the E/SE. Pocks for regeneration (D. fir and
p.pine) readily ignite.
• At 1305, the south flank continues to have good fuel consumption from firing operations. The north flank has been smoked in due to
downslope drafts. A wind change from the north occurred around this time.
• At 1811, winds are steady out of the west – timber & juniper are most receptive to ignitions. Lighters are bottom lighting big trees, maybe
firing patterns have contributed to increased mortality.
• At 2200, ignition operations were complete on the south flank. The crews plan to allow the fire to back down the slopes into the steeper
draws overnight.
Some overall fire behavior observations were recorded post-burn on day 3.
• More than 30% scorch (including trees less than 30”) on south aspect. Overall, scorch was estimated at 40%.
• North aspect: Overall scorch is 70%.
• Canopy trees of all sizes, 30% or more green of all size classes remain. \xbd of the canopy is greater than 9” dbh.
Lion Coulee EAST Unit 2: (Narrative provided by Jennifer Walker)
• Needle litter carried fire nicely except during early mornings. Adequate consumption of 1hr and 10hr fuels.
• Herbaceous green-up was advanced (cool season grasses were in flowering stage), but old litter carried fire through green during daytime
operations. Even so, ignitions generally had to focus on more receptive fuels in timbered areas. Spotting occurred in the bottom of Lion
Coulee during mop-up ignitions midday on 6/13 when the fuel moisture dropped to 2% at 82oF for a probability of ignition of 100%. There was
some cheat-grass in the bottom.
• All conifers were actively growing from recent bud-break so were reluctant to sustain fire; but plentiful juniper ladder fuels with needle litter
contributed to isolated torching of canopy trees. There were very long lag periods for heat buildup prior to torch-outs, so igniters had difficulty
judging the timing of their dots/strips. The isolated torching contributed to scorching of adjacent trees and associated mortality of those trees.
NOTES: In this mixed fire regime of DF, PP, and juniper, consider increasing the mortality objective for big trees. Or instead, use a crown
replacement objective for ~20% (or other appropriate) of unit.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The BLM has identified two units for treatment. The East Unit, totaling approximately 730 acres, contains mature stands of ponderosa pine and Douglas fir with a dense understory of small diameter conifers and juniper. In this unit, fire would be used to reduce understory fuels and provide fuel breaks in areas with a closed, continuous canopy. The West Unit, 960 acres in size, contains areas of heavy fuel loading as a result of blowdown from a summer Tornado that went through the area in 2002. It is proposed to treat about 50-70% of a unit providing a mosaic of burn intensities and vegetative diversity.

Actual_Implementation:
There was no FEMO on Day 1, so there are no photos or documented fire behavior observations. This narrative is from
Walker's observations in combination with Krage&$s weather documentation.
Grass had greened to about 6" height. Some p-pine had begun to break bud. Needle litter was damp in the morning
and dry in the afternoon.
Early in the day, jackpot fuels were targeted to achieve objectives. Fire behavior was minimal so igniters spot-fired
pine stringers in coulees.
As the day progressed, fire carried readily in green grass with cure and strip-firing was used in some locations to bring
black along with the lighters. Winds were terrain-driven and caused isolated torching where a.m. behavior would not.
There were no photo points in this portion of Unit D.

Midmorning conditions were drier than Day 1. Test fire ignitions at 0930 in needle/grass litter carried fairly well
except in areas with light fuel loads in green grass. Backing fire through needle litter achieved objectives nicely; p-pine
seedlings and juniper in grassy areas experienced scorching or isolated torching. Scorch heights in canopy trees was
generally less than 1 O&$ and rarely up to 20&$.
At 1400, 1-hr fuel moisture (calculated) dropped to 3% with a Pl of 80%. Fire behavior was meeting treatment
objectives, but ignitions were stopped and the line was checked because prescribed fire parameters were exceeded.
By 1600, calculated fuel moistures were within prescription, and at 1700 ignitions were resumed. Fire behavior was
active until after 1900.
At 2000 fuel moistures rose to 9% and ignitions targeted jackpot fuels until ignitions were complete.

Test fire was initiated at about 1000 under drier conditions than Day 2. Fire carried readily in the needle litter, backing
at about 6&& /min. Pine seedlings readily torched if ignited. Large trees scorch heights were 5&$ to 10&$, sometimes 20&$.
Treatment objectives were achieved, but were anticipated to exceed large tree mortality as conditions became warmer
and drier. Ignitions were stopped at about 1100.
By 1200, weather observations had exceeded prescribed fire parameters. Another spot Wx was requested at - 1500
which indicated RH recoveries would allow evening/nighttime ignitions. By 1600 weather conditions were within
prescription parameters and ignitions were resumed, but shifting wind from the north again shut down operations at
about 1800.
At - 1900 ignitions were resumed in the southern end of the unit with a new test fire . Fire effects achieved treatment
objectives, so operations continued and were completed by about 2 100. Isolated torching occurred from  firing=
until about 1930, after which strip-firing was required to produce isolated torching of juniper and seedling pockets.

Planned_Implementation:
A. Ground Based Ignition:
All operations will be managed by an RXB2. Various firing techniques including strip, backing, flanking,
and head fires will be used depending on fuels, weather, topography, and observed fire behavior. The
RXB2/FIRB will select the best firing pattern(s) that will provide for safety, minimize escape potential and
smoke impacts, and meet objectives. Initial operations will focus on using manmade and natural barriers,
along with areas of sparse fuels, to confine the fire to the unit and begin backing or flanking the fire down
slope, and/or, into the wind as necessary in order to establish black lines. As black lines obtain sufficient
depth for control purposes, interior ignition will begin and may utilize a variety of ignition patterns such as
strip head or chevron firing in order to generate the desired fire behavior. Holding resources may assist
with ignition operations as allowable. Generally, ignition operations will progress from the top of the slope
downward, and/or into the wind, until tying into the bottom of the coulee(s) or an established control line.
Interior two track roads, natural barriers, and constructed control lines within the units will provide for
burning the units in sections over the course of several days as/if needed. The fire's edge will be secured
at the end of each operational shift. Ignition may be conducted using drip torches, ATV/UTV torches,
fusees, and flare lanchers.
B. Simultaneous Ground based and Aerial Ignition:
A test fire will be conducted by ground crews, on the uphill and/or downwind side of the unit as directed
by the RXB2/FIRB. If results are satisfactory, firing will commence into the wind and/or down slope in
order to initiate a backing fire and to begin establishing black lines. Black lining may be conducted by the
holding forces and will consist of an ignition team progressing along each flank. As black lines attain
sufficient depth, or it becomes apparent that the majority of the burn unit perimeter will not support fire
spread due to sparse, and/or green fuels, aerial ignition of the interior may begin at the direction of the
Burn Boss/Fl RB. The aerial ignition operation will concentrate on target fuels within the interior of the unit
and will consist of running strips on the contour across the slope, beginning at the top and progressing
down slope and/or up wind whenever possible. The preferred sequence for aerial ignition of the interior
would be to lag behind black lining operations, and progress down slope toward coulee bottom(s) or
established control lines. Communication between ground and aerial resources will be maintained at all
times for safety and to coordinate between ignition and holding forces. Firing will continue along the
flanks of the unit as directed by the RXBB/FIRB. Aerial ignition may be completed using a PSD or
helitorch.
Actual_Implementation: The unit was blacklined by hand crews, followed by a helicopter used to finish ignition in the interior of the unit. The helicopter was funded by contributions from RMEF.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: Prescribed fire will be used to reduce natural fuel loadings and improve or maintain Fire Regime Condition Class (FRCC) in the project area. Mixed age Ponderosa stands in the project area vary from open stands to closed stands with thick understory and scattered pockets of conifer seedlings becoming established under the mature over story and encroaching into adjacent rangelands. Treatment in timber vegetation types will target juniper, small diameter conifers and seedlings, and surface fuels. Treatment in adjacent rangelands will reduce conifer encroachment and increase species variability in herbaceous cover. Prescribed fire will be applied in a manner that creates low to moderate intensity surface fire with\r\noccasional single and group tree torching into the forest canopy

Objectives:
The prescribed fire objectives of this project would be to:
I. Under burn a minimum 75 percent of the ponderosa stands.
2. Top-kill 30-60 percent of conifers less than 3" dbh (diameter at breast height)
3. Limit mortality in trees 8&& dbh and larger to 30 percent.
Planned_Implementation:
Prescribed fire operations would be conducted under specific conditions which result in low to moderate fire
intensity and create a mosaic of burned and unburned areas. Small trees and those encroaching on open areas would
be reduced while minimizing the risk to the mature overstory. The conditions under which prescribed fire would be
used and implemented would be addressed in a project-specific burn plan.
Actual_Implementation:
On April 9, 2012 ignition began for the “MIDDLE BLOCK” portion of Unit B. The test fire was initiated at 15:12
pm. Test fire results were favorable so continued hand-lighting along the unit boundary for a solid black line to
reinforce holding operations for the planned aerial ignition to begin the following day. At 19:00 the black-lining
operations were completed. On April 10, 2012 the aerial ignition test fire was initiated at 13:00 utilizing a Plastic
Sphere Dispenser (PSD) and Helicopter N910BR (Central Air Service). Fire carried readily in the grass and pine
seedlings and saplings torched if ignited. Occasional wind gusts briefly exceeded prescription, but sustained winds
were well within prescription and fire was meeting resource objectives, so decision was to continue with operations.
Aerial ignition on the MIDDLE BLOCK was completed at 17:00. The firing pattern of “flanking fire” did not meet
objectives, so the decision was made to “strip head fire” which did meet resource objectives.
On April 21, 2012 ignition began on the final phase of the unit – the “WEST BLOCK” at 12:02 pm by hand lighting
to create black-line along the unit boundary. The test fire carried well in the decadent grass but stopped where green-up
was occurring. The sage-brush had moderate consumption and isolated torching occurred in the pine seedlings and
saplings. Aerial ignition began by PSD began at 15:19.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The purpose of the proposed action is to shift the vegetation structure and composition in
the Tin Can Hill project area to fall within the historical fire regime. The current condition is an abundance of polesized
trees 5 - 9 inches diameter at breast height (dbh) and 9 - 21 inches dbh. The need for action is for a healthy
diverse forest that is within the historical fire regime. Timber stands are overstocked and poles and saplings are
encroaching on adjacent rangeland, due to departure from historical fire frequency. Improvements to the overall
condition class within the project area will likely result in benefits to wildlife habitat through an increase in the
diversity and production of herbaceous vegetation .
